newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe privatisation plan seen gathering steam.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe privatisation plan seen gathering steam.

text.p: The Zimbabwean government's decision to sell a majority stake in the ailing national steelworks marks a new commitment by Harare to implement a long-delayed privatisation plan, analysts said on Friday.

But some of the economic analysts said the government's preoccupation with black economic empowerment might still hinder the plan which has been on the cards since the government embarked on Western-backed reforms in 1991.

"We think it's the start of a new era where at least government is doing something about privatisation. Over the years there's just been talk about it but now there's something positive being done," said Kenias Mafukidze, president of the Zimbabwe Economic Society.
"It gives us hope that they will privatise more of the parastatals (state firms)," Mafukidze told Reuters.

Private consultants Coopers and Lybrand told Reuters this week that the government planned to give up a majority of its 90 percent shareholding in Zisco, one of Africa's largest integrated steelworks, under a part-privatisation plan aimed at injecting new life into the ailing firm.

The sale of the loss-making group, which has been plagued for years by management, production and cash problems and has stayed afloat on huge state subsidies, is being advertised in local and international media.

On Wednesday, Sanjeev Chhugani of Coopers and Lybrand -- consultants for the part-privatisation programme -- said bid documents for the sale would be released next Tuesday and submissions would close on April 16.

"It (the Zisco sale) would seem to signal a shift in policy because time and again ministers, even the president, have said they are not going to privatise," said Anthony Hawkins of Harare's University of Zimbabwe.

Hawkins and private economic consultant John Robertson said increasing pressure from Western donors for the government of President Robert Mugabe to divest from a host of state firms had also pushed it to make the decision.

They however added the pace of the privatisation programme would depend on how the government handled concerns from black economic empowerment groups pushing for a bigger stake in the economy, which they say is dominated by the country's white minority population.
"What clouds the whole issue of privatisation is indigenisation (black empowerment) which has been misdirected and misunderstood," Robertson said.

"The indigenisation objectives that were tied to Zisco interfered with the objectives of sorting out its problems. Now the government has finally accepted that Zisco is beyond the scope of indigenous businesspeople they are letting go.
"If they continue putting up indigenisation as a primary objective in the privatisation process it will quite likely seize up the process again," he added.
